title: Atlantis's rebellion and the flood

as_told.title: The rebellion in Atlantis recounted by Plato

tellings.quote: but when the divine portion began to fade away, and became diluted too often and too much with the mortal admixture, and the human nature got the upper hand, they then, being unable to bear their fortune, behaved unseemly, and to him who had an eye to see grew visibly debased, for they were losing the fairest of their precious gifts; but to those who had no eye to see the true happiness, they appeared glorious and blessed at the very time when they were full of avarice and unrighteous power.

Zeus, the god of gods, who rules according to law, and is able to see into such things, perceiving that an honourable race was in a woeful plight, and wanting to inflict punishment on them, that they might be chastened and improve, collected all the gods into their most holy habitation, which, being placed in the centre of the world, beholds all created things. And when he had called them together, he spake as follows--

But afterwards there occurred violent earthquakes and floods; and in a single day and night of misfortune all your warlike men in a body sank into the earth, and the island of Atlantis in like manner disappeared in the depths of the sea.

plain: The story goes that the people of Atlantis, a great island civilisation, turned against the gods, and Zeus, king of the Greek gods, punished them with a flood. The philosopher Jason Jorjani tells Michels that, according to the Greek philosopher Plato, the Atlanteans' 'great sin' was that they stopped sacrificing to the gods and worshipping them. Zeus then called the Olympian gods together 'and decides to wipe the world clean in what we more commonly know as Noah's flood'. At another point in the same talk Jorjani speaks of 'some rebellion in Atlantis', which he says Plato recounts in his dialogues the Timaeus and the Critias. Jorjani is the only teller on the show, and the other voice here is Plato's own text. In Benjamin Jowett's English translation of the Critias, the Atlanteans fall when 'the divine portion began to fade away' in them and they grow 'full of avarice and unrighteous power'. That is a fault of greed and decline, where Jorjani names a halt to sacrifice. Zeus, 'wanting to inflict punishment on them, that they might be chastened and improve', gathers the gods, but the text breaks off just as he starts to speak, so what he decided is not in it. The Timaeus tells the sinking without its cause: 'violent earthquakes and floods' came, and 'in a single day and night of misfortune' Atlantis 'disappeared in the depths of the sea'. Joining the two dialogues into a flood sent as punishment is a reading they invite, and calling it Noah's flood is Jorjani's own comparison. If his reading holds, the Atlantis tale and the biblical flood would be two memories of a single divine punishment.

discussion.text: In Jowett's translation of the Critias, the Atlanteans' fault is that "the divine portion began to fade away" in them and they grew "full of avarice and unrighteous power", where the teller names their ceasing to sacrifice to the gods; Zeus, "wanting to inflict punishment on them, that they might be chastened and improve", calls the gods together, and the text breaks off as he begins to speak, so what he decided is not in it. A flood sent for that fault is the teller's completion of the story, and calling it Noah's flood is his comparison; the text neither states nor excludes either.

In Jowett's translation of the Timaeus, Atlantis sank when "violent earthquakes and floods" came "in a single day and night of misfortune", after its war with Athens, and the Athenian warriors sank into the earth with it; the passage tells the sinking without its cause. The cause is told in the Critias, where Zeus calls the gods together to punish the Atlanteans' decline, and joining the two dialogues into a flood sent for a rebellion is a reading they invite, its last step, from punishment to flood, the teller's.
